newsitem.title: USA: Former banker Bynum faces Florida perjury charge.
newsitem.headline: Former banker Bynum faces Florida perjury charge.

text.p: A former Arkansas investment banker who pleaded guilty to bribing a Florida municipal official now faces a perjury charge accusing him of lying to a grand jury, federal officials said Tuesday.
The perjury indictment against Preston Bynum was returned in November 1995 but remained sealed until Feb. 6, when federal prosecutors sought its release.
Gail Kinsley, a spokeswoman for the U.S. Attorney's Office, said the government "absolutely" would proceed with prosecuting Bynum on the perjury charge.
"Now that the indictment is unsealed the government will go forth on the charges," she said.

Bynum resigned from Little Rock, Ark., investment banking firm Stephens Inc after pleading guilty in March 1995 to a bribery charge. He admitted he paid Terry Busbee, a former commissioner with the Escambia County Utility Authority, $67,200 in loans and cash to steer municipal bond underwriting business to Stephens Inc.
Neither Bynum nor the attorney who represented him in the earlier case could be reached for comment.
The firm underwrote two issues for the authority in 1992, while Busbee was a utility comissioner, but no one else at Stephens Inc was accused of wrongdoing.

The perjury indictment alleges that Bynum lied when he told the grand jury that loans he helped arrange for Busbee were supposed to have been used to pay Bert Brown, who had been hired as a consultant for Stephens Inc but had since died.
The indictment said Bynum knew that the money was "for the use and benefit of Terry D. Busbee" and not for Brown. It noted that most of the payments were made after Brown died.
The prosecutor who asked that the indictment be unsealed was unavailable for comment and it was unclear why the charge had been sealed.

Bynum served two years in prison on the criminal charge. He was also barred from the securities industry for life and fined $25,000 in an agrement to settle a civil fraud charge brought by the Securities and Exchange Commission in 1995.
The agency said Bynum and Busbee committed fraud by failing to disclose the illegal relationship.
Busbee was not fined because he demonstrated that he could not pay, and was not barred because he did not work for a regulated entity.
Busbee pleaded guilty in the criminal case to one bribery count and an income tax evasion charge. He was sentenced to 27 months in prison.
